note: Paraphrased, source-linked principles for a FICTIONAL office evacuation exercise. Not a complete legal or compliance program, not certified training, not advice for a real building. Federal OSHA text is a U.S. government work; NC DOL pages are cited for state context. Each card was checked against the linked page on 2026-10-17; exercise policies updated 2026-10-18 for the ground-floor map (office-v2) (ALARM-SYSTEM added for ruleset 2: pull stations, spreading fire, electrical door failures).

cards.title: Report emergencies; alarm employees
cards.principle: Where an OSHA standard requires an emergency action plan, the plan must include procedures for reporting a fire or other emergency, and the employer must have and maintain an employee alarm system that uses a distinctive signal for each purpose.
cards.exercise_policy: Reporting is simulated three ways: whoever first sees or smells fire shouts "Fire!" to their own room (an engine instinct, labelled as such); the notify tool is speech and reaches only people in the same room (doorways join the two rooms they connect), used to share what someone saw and where; and the pull_alarm tool at either of the two manual pull stations (main hallway, reception) is the building alarm — the only way to alert people in other rooms, and it says nothing about where the hazard is. No external message or real emergency call is ever sent.

cards.title: Employee alarm systems and manual pull stations
cards.principle: An employee alarm system must provide warning for the emergency action called for in the emergency action plan, be perceivable above ambient noise or light levels by all employees in the affected portions of the workplace (tactile devices may be used for employees who could not otherwise recognize it), and be distinctive and recognizable as a signal to evacuate. Manual actuation devices (pull stations) must be unobstructed, conspicuous and readily accessible, and back-up means of alarm such as employee runners or telephones are required when a system is out of service.
cards.exercise_policy: Two manual pull stations: one in the main hallway by the west exit, one in reception by the main entrance. Anyone who passes one on their way out pulls it by instinct; the planner can also send someone there and call pull_alarm. The siren and strobes alert every person to evacuate but convey no location — people learn where the fire or failed door is from what they see or are told in person. Nobody walks back into the building to reach the alarm once they are outside.

cards.title: Evacuation procedures and exit route assignments
cards.principle: The plan must include procedures for emergency evacuation, including type of evacuation and exit route assignments, and the employer must review the plan with each covered employee when it is developed or the employee is first assigned, when their responsibilities change, and when the plan changes.
cards.exercise_policy: Every character is briefed on the fictional primary and alternate routes and the assembly point. Current observations override the briefing when a route becomes unavailable. Fire can climb walls and spread through the building, and smoke can be noticed through a nearby wall; people back away from nearby flames by instinct, choose exits away from the fire, and never go back inside once they are out.

cards.title: Designated, trained evacuation assistants
cards.principle: An employer must designate and train employees to assist in a safe and orderly evacuation of other employees.
cards.exercise_policy: Alex is the modeled trained warden and buddy. Assistance requires the person's request (consent) and co-location. No carrying, lifting or improvised rescue action exists.

cards.title: Account for all employees after evacuation
cards.principle: The plan must include procedures to account for all employees after evacuation.
cards.exercise_policy: Check-in only counts when a character is physically inside the fictional assembly area; the warden's roster verification is the only way the exercise can be confirmed complete. People caught by the spreading fire are reported as lost, never assumed safe.

cards.title: Exit doors open from inside without keys
cards.principle: Employees must be able to open an exit route door from the inside at all times without keys, tools, or special knowledge.
cards.exercise_policy: All three exits in the fictional office (west exit, kitchen back exit, main entrance) are manual doors that always open from inside; they are deliberately not electrical, so a power failure cannot lock anyone in. Only the seven interior electric sliding doors (server room, Red Hat room, pantry, kitchen, cubicles, reception and the reception side door) can fail in the exercise. A locked exit is never used as a puzzle.

cards.title: Exit routes free and unobstructed
cards.principle: Exit routes must be free and unobstructed; no materials or equipment may be placed, either permanently or temporarily, within the exit route.
cards.exercise_policy: An Electrical failure that jams an interior sliding door shut is an abnormal exercise condition, never a recommended layout. Movement stops before the stuck door and returns ROUTE_UNAVAILABLE, so the planner must report it and re-route.

cards.title: Wardens know the layout, alternate routes and buddy arrangements
cards.section: Emergency Preparedness: Getting Started — Evacuation Wardens; Assisting Visitors and Workers to Evacuate
cards.principle: OSHA guidance (not a standard) suggests wardens be trained in the complete workplace layout and alternative escape routes if the primary route becomes blocked, that workers be made aware of workers with special needs who may require extra assistance, and how to use the buddy system.
cards.exercise_policy: Alex (warden) is the designated buddy for Daniel if Daniel asks for it. Daniel stays an active participant: he moves himself, communicates, and chooses whether to accept help.

cards.title: Assembly areas and head count
cards.section: Emergency Preparedness: Getting Started — Accounting for Workers after an Evacuation
cards.principle: OSHA guidance (not a standard) suggests designating assembly areas and taking a head count after the evacuation.
cards.exercise_policy: The fictional office has one outdoor assembly point — the bus stop across the street, reached over the crosswalk from every exit; the warden's roster verification is the head count.

cards.title: North Carolina context
cards.section: NC DOL OSH: Emergency Action Plans — Which standards apply?
cards.principle: NC DOL's OSH Division lists 29 CFR 1910.38 (emergency action plans) among the standards it has adopted that apply to emergency action plans in North Carolina general industry. Separately, NC DOL states North Carolina is an OSHA-approved State Plan and, with certain exceptions, adopts federal OSHA standards verbatim (labor.nc.gov/which-osha-standards-apply).
cards.exercise_policy: Context only. Whether a plan is required depends on the specific workplace and standard; this exercise makes no claim that the fictional office or its plan is compliant.
